RE: 2026 CMS Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs 
Proposed Rule (CMS-0062-P) 
 
Dear Administrator Oz and National Coordinator Keane: 
 
The Infusion Providers Alliance (IPA) is pleased to provide comments on CMS’s   
2026 Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs Proposed Rule (CMS-
0062-P). 
 
IPA strongly supports CMS’s efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization 
processes for drugs, including drugs covered under the medical beneﬁt. Prior 
authorization, as well as other utilization management tools, has become a signiﬁcant 
administrative burden for community-based physician practices and ambulatory infusion 
centers. Submitting and processing authorizations can delay medically necessary 
treatment and increase costs for providers and patients.  
 
Speciﬁcally, CMS proposes to require impacted payers to support electronic prior 
authorization, to make decisions on requests within shorter timeframes that align CMS 
programs, and to increase transparency for the prior authorization of drugs. IPA supports 
the proposed rule. It is an important step forward toward more timely and efficient care, 
which should improve patient access by removing unnecessary administrative burdens.     
 
More broadly, IPA believes that prior authorization, when necessary, should be used to 
conﬁrm that a patient has a diagnosed condition for which a prescribed therapy is 
medically appropriate, rather than as a mechanism to direct treatment decisions, mandate 
particular distribution channels, or otherwise interfere with physician-directed care.  
 
IPA also encourages CMS to continue identifying opportunities to reduce unnecessary 
administrative complexity and improve the efficiency, transparency, and predictability of 
the prior authorization process for patients and providers.  
 
With respect to the proposed rule, IPA offers comments on the following proposals and 
requests for information: 
 
1. Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs;  
2. CMS’s Proposed Denial Explanation Requirements;  
3. Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes;  
4. Additional Opportunities to Reduce Administrative Burden with Prior Authorization;  
5. Request for Information (RFI) on Increasing Health Care Resiliency.   
 
Background on the Infusion Providers Alliance 
 
The Infusion Providers Alliance (IPA) is a leading voice for community-based, non-hospital 
affiliated physician practices and freestanding ambulatory infusion clinics that administer 
complex biologic therapies to patients in the lowest cost, clinically appropriate settings of 
care. IPA members operate over 1,000 sites across 45 states. IPA is committed to 
preserving the integrity of the provider-patient relationship in a manner that delivers 
exceptional care to patients and value to the health care system. Studies have shown that 
care delivered in these settings is superior to other sites of care1 while also generating 
savings compared with administering the same drug infusion in hospital outpatient 
departments (HOPDs)2, typically saving Medicare more than $200 per Part B drug infusion 
encounter.  
 
IPA member facilities are major access points for care in communities large and small. 
Located where patients live and work, they provide ﬂexible, convenient access to treatment 
for conditions such as Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid 
 
1 Raj L, Stinson G, Langsam JW, DeMacio J. Comparison of specialty injection and infusion adverse events 
among hospital outpatient settings vs non-hospital outpatient settings. J Clin Pathways. 2025;11(1):34-38. 
doi:10.25270/jcp.2025.11.01 
2 JMCP, Infusion Therapy Patient Outcomes Are Similar at Reduced Costs (Dec. 20, 2025), 
https://www.jmcp.org/doi/10.18553/jmcp.2025.25264 
arthritis, and many other chronic, complex, and rare conditions. IPA’s mission is to serve as 
a thought leader and to educate on issues critical to safeguarding, supporting, and 
strengthening provider-directed, patient-focused access to infused medications. More 
information about IPA can be found on our website: www.infusionprovidersalliance.org. 
 
Electronic Prior Authorization for Drugs  
IPA strongly supports efforts to streamline and modernize prior authorization processes 
because we are focused ﬁrst and foremost on providing the right drug treatment to the right 
patient at the right time. Unfortunately, our patients routinely experience denials and 
signiﬁcant delays in obtaining drug treatments prescribed by their physicians due to 
unnecessary and onerous prior authorization requirements imposed by payers. Moreover, 
our infusion centers experience signiﬁcant administrative burdens associated with 
obtaining prior authorizations for medically necessary therapies. 
These burdens are particularly acute for physician practices and freestanding infusion 
centers which typically operate with limited staffing resources, unlike hospitals that can 
redeploy nurses and support staff from other departments based on workﬂow changes. 
For patients with chronic and complex conditions requiring infused biologic therapies, 
delays associated with prior authorization can result in postponed treatment, disease 
progression, and ﬂare-ups that may result in avoidable hospitalizations.  
IPA therefore supports CMS’s efforts to expand electronic prior authorization 
requirements to drugs. These reforms should reduce manual submissions, standardize 
data exchange requirements, and minimize duplicative administrative processes between 
providers and payers. We concur with CMS’s statement that aligning the technology and 
standards for all items, services, and drugs covered under a medical beneﬁt would 
streamline the prior authorization process for providers and patients, enable real-time data 
exchange, improve electronic documentation submission, and accelerate payers’ ability to 
make decisions. 
CMS’s Proposed Denial Explanation Requirements 
IPA supports CMS’s proposal requiring Medicaid, Children's Health Insurance Program 
(CHIP), and Qualiﬁed Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally-facilitated Exchanges 
(FFEs) to provide a speciﬁc reason when denying prior authorization requests for 
drugs. 
Transparency of denial rationales is essential to ensuring that prior authorization remains 
focused on medical necessity and clinical appropriateness. Providers and patients should 
have access to clear information regarding the basis for a denial so they can understand 
the determination, evaluate next steps, and pursue appropriate appeals when necessary.  
IPA is concerned that some payers increasingly use prior authorization processes not 
solely to evaluate clinical appropriateness, but also to steer providers toward payer-
preferred products or specialty pharmacy arrangements that may disrupt physician-
directed treatment plans.  
Prior authorization should be used to conﬁrm that a patient has a diagnosed condition for 
which a prescribed therapy is medically appropriate. It should not create unnecessary 
barriers that interfere with physician-directed treatment decisions, mandate particular 
distribution channels, or force non-medical switching based on payer preferences.  
Physicians and their patients are generally best positioned to determine the most 
appropriate course of treatment based on individual clinical circumstances.  
Increased transparency and reporting around denial rationales can help identify 
inappropriate utilization management practices and provide greater accountability for how 
prior authorization requirements are applied. Greater visibility into denial patterns may 
also help policymakers, providers, and patients better understand whether prior 
authorization is being used primarily to evaluate clinical appropriateness or to advance 
other objectives unrelated to patient care.  
IPA supports CMS’s proposal to require speciﬁc explanations for prior authorization 
denials and believes the proposal represents an important step toward improving 
transparency, accountability, and patient access to medically necessary therapies.  
Prior Authorization Decision Timeframes 
 
Timely access to treatment is particularly important for patients receiving infused biologic 
therapies for chronic and complex conditions. Delays in treatment can adversely affect 
patient outcomes and may result in postponed treatment, disease progression, disease 
ﬂare-ups, and avoidable hospitalizations. 
 
IPA supports CMS's proposed prior authorization decision timeframes, including the 
proposed seven-calendar-day timeframe for standard prior authorization requests 
and the proposed 72-hour timeframe for expedited requests. IPA supports CMS's efforts 
to align prior authorization decision timeframes across coverage programs and payer types 
as this will promote greater consistency. Establishing consistent decision timeframes 
should improve predictability for providers and patients while helping ensure that 
medically necessary treatment is not delayed unnecessarily. 
 
IPA also encourages CMS to closely monitor compliance with applicable prior 
authorization decision timeframes across impacted payers to ensure that patients 
receiving physician-administered and other medically necessary therapies receive timely 
access to care. 
 
Additional Opportunities to Reduce Administrative Burden Associated 
with Prior Authorization  
While IPA supports CMS's efforts to modernize prior authorization processes, additional 
opportunities remain to reduce unnecessary administrative burden associated with prior 
authorization requirements. 
Patients may experience unnecessary disruptions in care when providers obtain prior 
authorization for medically necessary treatment, administer therapy consistent with that 
approval, and subsequently face claim denials for lack of medical records or other 
administrative documentation requests. This practice undermines the purpose of prior 
authorization and creates uncertainty for providers who have already complied with the 
requirements necessary to obtain authorization prior to treatment. In 2024, an IPA member 
experienced 8,000 denials for medical records where a prior authorization had previously 
been approved. 
IPA believes that providers should be able to rely on valid prior authorization approvals 
when furnishing medically necessary treatment. When a provider receives prior 
authorization approval, administers treatment consistent with the authorization, and 
submits a claim consistent with the authorization terms, providers should not be subjected 
to duplicative documentation requirements that effectively require them to re-establish the 
medical necessity determination that was already reviewed during the prior authorization 
process. 
Greater alignment between prior authorization approvals and subsequent claims 
processes would reduce unnecessary provider burden, improve payment predictability, 
and further advance the administrative simpliﬁcation goals underlying this proposed rule. 
IPA encourages CMS to continue examining opportunities to better align prior authorization 
approvals, documentation requirements, and subsequent claims adjudication processes. 
Increasing Health Care Resiliency 
 
CMS states that hacking, ransomware, and other cybersecurity attacks on health care 
systems and electronic protected health information (ePHI) present an ever-increasing 
threat. These attacks have already caused, and could continue to cause, signiﬁcant 
disruption to the health care industry, potentially resulting in signiﬁcant harm to patients, 
providers, payers, and the health care ecosystem at large. CMS seeks feedback on 
opportunities to strengthen, protect, and increase the resiliency of our health care system 
in cybersecurity spaces to prevent and better handle future threats. Additionally, CMS 
would like to hear about existing standards and technologies, as well as the current role of 
point-to-point connections within the health care system. 
 
Infusion providers welcome CMS focus on deterring these types of disruptions.  Our 
members were put under substantial economic duress from the 2024 hack to Change 
Healthcare due to their unique economic “buy-and-bill” model which requires infusion 
companies and physician practices to ﬁrst purchase very expensive drugs and then wait for 
a delayed payment to arrive.  While other providers were seeing payment delays for their 
professional services, infusion providers were also experiencing payment delays for 
fronting the payment. These providers were inventorying expensive biological drugs and 
maintaining adequate supply for administration to patients who could not delay their care 
and treatment regimens, all while payments were being delayed. This disruption also 
required a signiﬁcant increase in employee hours to address the administrative burden. 
There are some groups still recovering from the overall strain of this ransomware attack. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this important topic.  
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
Elliott Warren 
Executive Director 
Infusion Providers Alliance

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Infusion Providers Alliance (IPA); signed by Elliott Warren, Executive Director.
- **Stakeholder type:** Professional Association / Healthcare Provider association.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Represents community-based, non-hospital affiliated physician practices and freestanding ambulatory infusion clinics; members operate over 1,000 sites across 45 states and administer complex biologic therapies.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

IPA strongly supports CMS-0062-P, especially expansion of electronic prior authorization to drugs covered under the medical benefit, specific denial reasons, and aligned decision timeframes. IPA urges CMS to ensure prior authorization remains focused on medical necessity rather than payer steering, and to address duplicative post-authorization documentation and claims denials that undermine administrative simplification.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; TRANSPARENCY/API-related reporting generally; GENERAL/RFI on resiliency.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No specific CFR citations; references CMS-0062-P and the 2026 proposed rule.
- **Standards referenced:** Electronic prior authorization; FHIR alignment for medical benefit drugs is discussed generally; cybersecurity/resiliency standards are referenced conceptually.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Electronic prior authorization for medical benefit drugs**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Manual and inconsistent PA processes delay biologic infusions and create burdens for community practices and ambulatory infusion centers with limited staffing.
- **Specific request:** Finalize expansion of electronic PA requirements to drugs and align technology/standards for medical benefit drugs with the broader PA API framework.

**Topic 2: Specific denial explanations**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Clear denial rationales are needed for appeals, resubmissions, and accountability, especially where payers may be using PA to steer treatment or distribution channels.
- **Specific request:** Require specific denial explanations and improve transparency into denial patterns.

**Topic 3: Decision timeframes for drug prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Delays in infused biologic treatment can cause postponed treatment, disease progression, flares, and avoidable hospitalizations.
- **Specific request:** Finalize proposed seven-calendar-day standard and 72-hour expedited timeframes and monitor payer compliance.

**Topic 4: Reliance on valid prior authorization approvals**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Providers face claim denials and medical record requests even after valid prior authorization approvals, duplicating the medical necessity review.
- **Specific request:** Align PA approvals with subsequent claims adjudication and prevent duplicative documentation demands where care was furnished consistent with an authorization.

**Topic 5: Health care resiliency and cyber disruption**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI S66-S82
- **Position:** Support / Clarify
- **Rationale:** Infusion providers were economically strained by the 2024 Change Healthcare cyberattack due to buy-and-bill drug purchasing and payment delays.
- **Specific request:** Continue focusing on cybersecurity resilience and consider impacts on providers that carry high-cost drug inventory.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S12:** Supports addressing technical and workflow barriers for medical benefit drug ePA by expanding electronic PA requirements to medical benefit drugs.
- **S16:** Supports requiring specific reasons for drug PA denials so providers and patients can understand determinations and pursue appeals.
- **S17:** Implied support for more transparent and reportable denial rationales, though structured codes are not discussed in detail.
- **S20/S43:** Supports aligned and shorter decision timeframes for drug PA and monitoring compliance.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to the health care resiliency RFI by describing the economic and operational impact of the Change Healthcare ransomware attack on infusion providers.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize expansion of electronic prior authorization requirements to drugs, including medical benefit drugs.
2. Require specific, actionable reasons for drug PA denials.
3. Finalize and monitor compliance with proposed PA decision timeframes.
4. Ensure prior authorization is not used to mandate distribution channels, non-medical switching, or payer-preferred treatment decisions.
5. Prevent duplicative post-authorization documentation and claims denials when treatment matches an approved authorization.
6. Strengthen health care resiliency policies with attention to infusion providers' buy-and-bill vulnerabilities.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Administrative burden; treatment delays; opaque denial rationales; payer steering; duplicative documentation after PA approval; cybersecurity disruption.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Disease progression, flare-ups, avoidable hospitalizations, payment delays, increased employee hours, provider financial strain.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Limited staffing in community practices and freestanding infusion centers; fragmented PA and claims workflows; cyber disruptions to payment systems.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** IPA members operate over 1,000 sites in 45 states; infusion in lower-cost sites typically saves Medicare more than $200 per Part B drug infusion encounter; one member experienced 8,000 medical-record denials after PA approval in 2024.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Specialty injection/infusion adverse event comparison in J Clin Pathways; JMCP study on infusion therapy outcomes and reduced costs.
- **Examples provided:** Change Healthcare ransomware attack and its effect on infusion provider cash flow and staffing.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Infusion providers, physician practices, ambulatory infusion centers, patients with chronic/complex conditions, payers.
- **Economic implications:** Electronic PA and fewer duplicative denials could reduce administrative and payment uncertainty; cyber disruptions disproportionately affect buy-and-bill providers.
- **Technical feasibility:** Supportive of ePA modernization; does not raise major feasibility objections.
- **Patient care impact:** Strongly positive if finalized; faster access and clearer denials may reduce treatment delays and avoidable hospital use.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive
- **Tone:** Professional, provider-focused, collaborative
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "IPA strongly supports CMS’s efforts to modernize and streamline prior authorization processes for drugs, including drugs covered under the medical benefit." - Context: Overall support for the rule.
2. "Prior authorization should be used to confirm that a patient has a diagnosed condition for which a prescribed therapy is medically appropriate." - Context: Concern about payer steering and interference with physician-directed care.
3. "In 2024, an IPA member experienced 8,000 denials for medical records where a prior authorization had previously been approved." - Context: Evidence of duplicative burden after PA approval.
4. "There are some groups still recovering from the overall strain of this ransomware attack." - Context: Health care resiliency RFI response.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **IMPLEMENTATION-TIMELINE** - Supports timely decision deadlines and compliance monitoring.
- [x] **COST-RESOURCES** - Discusses cost savings from lower-cost infusion sites and burdens from duplicative denials and cyber disruption.
- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - Central theme; PA and post-PA documentation drain limited staffing resources.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Emphasizes delayed infused biologic therapies and avoidable hospitalizations.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Supports specific denial reasons and visibility into denial patterns.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Seeks alignment between PA approvals, documentation requests, and claims adjudication.
- [x] **PRIVACY-SECURITY** - Addresses cybersecurity and resiliency impacts from ransomware.
